claim: Many small endotherms use torpor to reduce metabolic rate and manage daily energy balance.
source: Many small endotherms use torpor to reduce metabolic rate and manage daily energy balance.
evidence: This is a general statement about small endotherms that draws from established scientific knowledge about torpor use.

claim: During the mid-summer, ruby-throated hummingbirds entered torpor at consistently low fat stores (~5% of body mass).
source: During the mid-summer, birds entered torpor at consistently low fat stores (~5% of body mass), and torpor duration was negatively related to evening fat load.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of body composition and torpor use in the study.

claim: Torpor duration was negatively related to evening fat load during mid-summer.
source: During the mid-summer, birds entered torpor at consistently low fat stores (~5% of body mass), and torpor duration was negatively related to evening fat load.
evidence: This relationship is demonstrated through respirometry and body composition measurements.

claim: During the migration period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on nights when they had higher fat stores.
source: During the migration period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on nights when they had higher fat stores, and fat gain was positively correlated with the amount of torpor used.
evidence: This finding is based on experimental observations during the migration period.

claim: Fat gain was positively correlated with the amount of torpor used during the migration period.
source: During the migration period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on nights when they had higher fat stores, and fat gain was positively correlated with the amount of torpor used.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated through measurements of body composition changes and torpor duration.

claim: There is a fundamental change in physiological feedback between adiposity and torpor during migration.
source: These findings demonstrate the versatility of torpor throughout the annual cycle and suggest a fundamental change in physiological feedback between adiposity and torpor during migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed reversal in the relationship between fat stores and torpor use between breeding and migration periods.

claim: Facultative heterothermy is underappreciated in migratory ecology.
source: Moreover, this study highlights the underappreciated importance of facultative heterothermy in migratory ecology.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader field based on the study's findings.

claim: Facultative hypothermia allows many mammalian and some avian species to survive periods of resource unavailability or to optimize their energy budgets.
source: Facultative hypothermia is an energy conservation strategy that allows many mammalian and some avian species to survive periods of resource unavailability or to optimize their energy budgets in certain environments or life stages (McKechnie and Lovegrove, 2002; Ruf and Geiser, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During facultative hypothermia, metabolic rates and body temperatures are reduced to varying extents across species and environmental conditions.
source: During facultative hypothermia, metabolic rates and body temperatures are reduced to varying extents across species and environmental conditions (Ruf and Geiser, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hummingbirds are some of the smallest avian species.
source: As some of the smallest avian species, hummingbirds (Trochilidae) are known for their ability to use daily torpor, a deep, short-term form of facultative hypothermia, to cope with energetic challenges they face daily and throughout their annual cycle (Carpenter, 1974; Hainsworth et al., 1977).
evidence: This is established knowledge about hummingbird body size.

claim: Hummingbirds are known for their ability to use daily torpor to cope with energetic challenges.
source: As some of the smallest avian species, hummingbirds (Trochilidae) are known for their ability to use daily torpor, a deep, short-term form of facultative hypothermia, to cope with energetic challenges they face daily and throughout their annual cycle (Carpenter, 1974; Hainsworth et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Daily torpor is a deep, short-term form of facultative hypothermia.
source: As some of the smallest avian species, hummingbirds (Trochilidae) are known for their ability to use daily torpor, a deep, short-term form of facultative hypothermia, to cope with energetic challenges they face daily and throughout their annual cycle (Carpenter, 1974; Hainsworth et al., 1977).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Torpor initiation in hummingbirds is controlled by an endogenous mechanism sensitive to an energy-store threshold.
source: Studies that have investigated the use of torpor in hummingbirds in relation to food availability and body mass suggest that torpor initiation is controlled by an endogenous mechanism sensitive to an energy-store threshold (Hainsworth et al., 1977; Hiebert, 1992; Powers et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A bird will initiate torpor if its energy stores reach critically low levels with enough time remaining in the night to achieve net energy savings.
source: This model predicts that a bird will initiate torpor if its energy stores reach critically low levels with enough time remaining in the night to achieve net energy savings.
evidence: This is a prediction from a model described in previous literature.

claim: Hummingbirds typically rewarm 1–2 hr before sunrise.
source: Hummingbirds typically rewarm 1–2 hr before sunrise, so they rarely enter torpor after approximately 75% of the night has elapsed; even if critically low energy levels are reached late in the night, birds may avoid entering torpor at this point if the energetic benefits are outweighed by the potential costs (e.g. predation, moult delay) (Bouma et al., 2010; Carr and Lima, 2013; Hainsworth et al., 1977; Hiebert, 1992; Hiebert, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hummingbirds rarely enter torpor after approximately 75% of the night has elapsed.
source: Hummingbirds typically rewarm 1–2 hr before sunrise, so they rarely enter torpor after approximately 75% of the night has elapsed; even if critically low energy levels are reached late in the night, birds may avoid entering torpor at this point if the energetic benefits are outweighed by the potential costs (e.g. predation, moult delay) (Bouma et al., 2010; Carr and Lima, 2013; Hainsworth et al., 1977; Hiebert, 1992; Hiebert, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Birds may avoid entering torpor late in the night if the energetic benefits are outweighed by potential costs such as predation or moult delay.
source: Hummingbirds typically rewarm 1–2 hr before sunrise, so they rarely enter torpor after approximately 75% of the night has elapsed; even if critically low energy levels are reached late in the night, birds may avoid entering torpor at this point if the energetic benefits are outweighed by the potential costs (e.g. predation, moult delay) (Bouma et al., 2010; Carr and Lima, 2013; Hainsworth et al., 1977; Hiebert, 1992; Hiebert, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The function of torpor shifts seasonally from an energy emergency survival mechanism to an energy-storage maximization strategy during migration.
source: Previous studies also suggest that the function of torpor shifts seasonally, from an energy emergency survival mechanism to an energy-storage maximization strategy during migration (Carpenter and Hixon, 1988; Hiebert, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The threshold for torpor initiation has not been repeatedly and accurately measured in individual birds spanning life history stages prior to this study.
source: However, this threshold has not been repeatedly and accurately measured in individual birds spanning life history stages, and the relationship between torpor use and the components of body composition (fat and lean mass) remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in previous research that the current study addresses.

claim: The relationship between torpor use and the components of body composition (fat and lean mass) remains unclear prior to this study.
source: However, this threshold has not been repeatedly and accurately measured in individual birds spanning life history stages, and the relationship between torpor use and the components of body composition (fat and lean mass) remains unclear.
evidence: This identifies a gap in previous research.

claim: Ruby-throated hummingbirds breed in eastern North America in the early and mid-summer.
source: We explored torpor use in ruby-throated hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), which breed in eastern North America in the early and mid-summer, and migrate to wintering grounds in Mexico and Central America in the late summer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the species' life history.

claim: Ruby-throated hummingbirds migrate to wintering grounds in Mexico and Central America in the late summer.
source: We explored torpor use in ruby-throated hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris), which breed in eastern North America in the early and mid-summer, and migrate to wintering grounds in Mexico and Central America in the late summer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the species' migration.

claim: In the breeding period, hummingbirds maintain relatively lean body compositions to optimize aerial agility.
source: In the breeding period, birds maintain relatively lean body compositions to optimize aerial agility, important for successful courtship displays and competitive interactions that allow them to maintain secure access to food resources (Altshuler et al., 2010; Hou and Welch, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Aerial agility is important for successful courtship displays and competitive interactions in hummingbirds.
source: In the breeding period, birds maintain relatively lean body compositions to optimize aerial agility, important for successful courtship displays and competitive interactions that allow them to maintain secure access to food resources (Altshuler et al., 2010; Hou and Welch, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ruby-throated hummingbirds substantially increase their body mass prior to migratory departure.
source: But like most long-distance migrants, ruby-throated hummingbirds substantially increase their body mass prior to migratory departure to fuel their journey (Hou and Welch, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Most long-distance migrants increase their body mass prior to migratory departure to fuel their journey.
source: But like most long-distance migrants, ruby-throated hummingbirds substantially increase their body mass prior to migratory departure to fuel their journey (Hou and Welch, 2016).
evidence: This is general knowledge about migratory birds supported by a citation.

claim: Thirteen of 16 birds exhibited relatively low morning body masses until late August or early September when they substantially increased their body mass.
source: Throughout the study period, 13 of 16 birds exhibited relatively low morning body masses, indicative of breeding condition, until late August or early September when they substantially increased their body mass; the birds subsequently maintained high body masses.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of body mass throughout the study.

claim: Changes in body mass were driven primarily by increases in fat.
source: QMR scans indicated that changes in body mass were driven primarily by increases in fat (r(109)=0.94, 95% CI [0.92, 0.96] p < 0.001; Appendix 1—figure 1A), and that body mass and lean mass were slightly negatively correlated (r(107)=−0.26, 95% CI [−0.43,–0.08], p = 0.006; Appendix 1—figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by QMR measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Body mass and lean mass were slightly negatively correlated.
source: QMR scans indicated that changes in body mass were driven primarily by increases in fat (r(109)=0.94, 95% CI [0.92, 0.96] p < 0.001; Appendix 1—figure 1A), and that body mass and lean mass were slightly negatively correlated (r(107)=−0.26, 95% CI [−0.43,–0.08], p = 0.006; Appendix 1—figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by QMR measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Individual variation in daily food consumption and activity were the primary factors leading to nightly variation in evening body composition.
source: Individual variation in daily food consumption and presumably activity were the primary factors leading to nightly variation in evening body composition, as environmental factors such as air temperature, humidity, and food availability were consistent throughout the study period.
evidence: This is inferred from the controlled experimental conditions.

claim: During the mid-summer breeding period, birds maintained consistently low morning body masses (2.77 ± 0.05 g).
source: During the mid-summer breeding period, birds maintained consistently low morning body masses (2.77 ± 0.05 g; slope: 0.00 ± 0.00 g⋅day–1; p = 0.338; Figure 1; Table 1; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Birds used torpor on 61.6% ± 11.1% of focal bird-nights during the breeding period.
source: On average, birds used torpor on 61.6% ± 11.1% of focal bird-nights (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on respirometry measurements during the breeding period.

claim: When birds started the night with less fat during the breeding period, they were more likely to enter torpor.
source: When birds started the night with less fat, they were more likely to enter torpor (slope: –0.70 ± 0.22; p = 0.001; Appendix 1—figure 2), entered torpor earlier in the night (slope: 0.55 ± 0.09 hentry ⋅%fat–1; p < 0.001), and remained torpid longer (slope: –0.63 ± 0.10 hr⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of respirometry and body composition data.

claim: When birds started the night with less fat during the breeding period, they entered torpor earlier in the night.
source: When birds started the night with less fat, they were more likely to enter torpor (slope: –0.70 ± 0.22; p = 0.001; Appendix 1—figure 2), entered torpor earlier in the night (slope: 0.55 ± 0.09 hentry ⋅%fat–1; p < 0.001), and remained torpid longer (slope: –0.63 ± 0.10 hr⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of respirometry and body composition data.

claim: When birds started the night with less fat during the breeding period, they remained torpid longer.
source: When birds started the night with less fat, they were more likely to enter torpor (slope: –0.70 ± 0.22; p = 0.001; Appendix 1—figure 2), entered torpor earlier in the night (slope: 0.55 ± 0.09 hentry ⋅%fat–1; p < 0.001), and remained torpid longer (slope: –0.63 ± 0.10 hr⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of respirometry and body composition data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During the breeding period, torpor propensity was not significantly related to night length.
source: Neither torpor propensity (slope: –0.31 ± 0.47, p = 0.452), the time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night (slope: 0.52 ± 0.30 hentry⋅hnight, p = 0.054) nor torpor duration (slope: 0.52 ± 0.32 htorpor⋅hnight, p = 0.077) were significantly related to night length (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: During the breeding period, the time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night was not significantly related to night length.
source: Neither torpor propensity (slope: –0.31 ± 0.47, p = 0.452), the time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night (slope: 0.52 ± 0.30 hentry⋅hnight, p = 0.054) nor torpor duration (slope: 0.52 ± 0.32 htorpor⋅hnight, p = 0.077) were significantly related to night length (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: During the breeding period, torpor duration was not significantly related to night length.
source: Neither torpor propensity (slope: –0.31 ± 0.47, p = 0.452), the time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night (slope: 0.52 ± 0.30 hentry⋅hnight, p = 0.054) nor torpor duration (slope: 0.52 ± 0.32 htorpor⋅hnight, p = 0.077) were significantly related to night length (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: When birds started the night with greater fat content during the breeding period, they expended more energy before initiating torpor.
source: Furthermore, when birds started the night with greater fat content, they expended more energy before initiating torpor (slope: 0.39 ± 0.06 kJ⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001, Appendix 1—figure 3A), and lost more fat mass overnight (slope: 9.98 ± 1.76 mgfat⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of respirometry data.

claim: When birds started the night with greater fat content during the breeding period, they lost more fat mass overnight.
source: Furthermore, when birds started the night with greater fat content, they expended more energy before initiating torpor (slope: 0.39 ± 0.06 kJ⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001, Appendix 1—figure 3A), and lost more fat mass overnight (slope: 9.98 ± 1.76 mgfat⋅%fat–1, p < 0.001; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of body composition data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: On longer nights during the breeding period, birds spent significantly more energy before entering torpor.
source: Additionally, on longer nights, birds spent significantly more energy before entering torpor (slope: 0.40 ± 0.22 kJ⋅hnight–1, p = 0.041), and lost more fat (slope: 13.5 ± 5.97 mgfat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.014).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of respirometry data.

claim: On longer nights during the breeding period, birds lost more fat.
source: Additionally, on longer nights, birds spent significantly more energy before entering torpor (slope: 0.40 ± 0.22 kJ⋅hnight–1, p = 0.041), and lost more fat (slope: 13.5 ± 5.97 mgfat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.014).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of body composition data.

claim: Throughout the breeding period, birds consistently entered torpor at a relatively low remaining fat level (5.56% ± 0.79%; 142.84 ± 39.17 mgfat).
source: Throughout the breeding period, birds consistently entered torpor at a time when they had a relatively low remaining fat level (5.56% ± 0.79%; 142.84 ± 39.17 mgfat; Figure 3B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on calculated fat content at torpor entry shown in Figure 3B.

claim: During the breeding period, the fat content at the time of torpor entry did not vary with night length.
source: The fat content at the time of torpor entry did not vary with night length (slope: 0.84 ± 0.78 %fat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.253), or the time of torpor entry (slope: 0.38% ± 0.31% fat⋅hentry–1; p = 0.191; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: During the breeding period, the fat content at the time of torpor entry did not vary with the time of torpor entry.
source: The fat content at the time of torpor entry did not vary with night length (slope: 0.84 ± 0.78 %fat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.253), or the time of torpor entry (slope: 0.38% ± 0.31% fat⋅hentry–1; p = 0.191; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Birds never entered torpor after approximately 75% of the night had elapsed, except on one night in which the bird entered torpor at 80% of the night and aroused within 1 hr.
source: Consistent with published observations, birds never entered torpor after approximately 75% of the night had elapsed, except on one night in which the bird entered torpor at 80% of the night and aroused within 1 hr (Hiebert, 1992; Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3 and consistent with previous research.

claim: On 47 of 55 (85%) bird-nights during the breeding period, the birds either entered torpor when their fat contents reached approximately 5% of body mass, or did not enter torpor if their fat content passed this threshold after 75% of the night had elapsed.
source: On 47 of 55 (85%) bird-nights, the birds either entered torpor when their fat contents reached approximately 5% of body mass, or did not enter torpor if their fat content passed this threshold after 75% of the night had elapsed (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: In late August and September, 13 of 16 birds increased body mass over the span of 10 ± 1 days (range: 6–18 days).
source: In late August and September, 13 of 16 birds increased body mass (slope: 0.02 ± 0.00 g⋅day–1, p < 0.001; Supplementary file 1A) over the span of 10 ± 1 days (range: 6–18 days; Figure 1; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is based on body mass measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: During the fattening period, birds increased body mass by an average of 0.58 ± 0.05 g (range: 0.34–0.90 g).
source: In this short period, birds increased body mass by an average of 0.58 ± 0.05 g (range: 0.34–0.90 g).
evidence: This is based on body mass measurements during the fattening period.

claim: Relative to the start of fattening, birds increased their body mass by an average of 19.6% ± 1.6% (range: 11.6–29.0%).
source: Relative to the start of fattening, birds increased their body mass by an average of 19.6% ± 1.6% (range: 11.6–29.0%; Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is based on body mass measurements during the fattening period.

claim: In every period, there was a negative relationship between torpor duration and overnight fat mass loss.
source: In every period, there was a negative relationship between torpor duration and overnight fat mass loss (slopes: breeding: –17.23 ± 0.52 mgfat⋅hr–1, fattening: –16.82 ± 1.02 mgfat⋅hr–1, migration: –15.35 ± 0.72 mgfat⋅hr–1, p < 0.001; Appendix 1—figure 4; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of body composition and torpor data across all periods.

claim: Longer torpor durations invariably spared more fat.
source: Because longer torpor durations invariably spared more fat, we predicted that more frequent and longer torpor use, in addition to higher food consumption during the fattening period, would enhance the rate of premigratory fattening.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative relationship between torpor duration and fat loss.

claim: Birds that used torpor for longer on average achieved greater mass gains during the fattening period.
source: Most interestingly, birds that used torpor for longer on average achieved greater mass gains during the fattening period (slope: 0.07 ± 0.01 g⋅hr–1; p = 0.004; n = 11; Figure 4A; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Food consumption did not significantly affect the amount of fattening.
source: Contrary to our predictions, food consumption did not significantly affect the amount of fattening (slope: 0.00 ± 0.00 g⋅kJ–1, p = 0.996), and neither mean torpor duration (slope: –0.60 ± 0.75 days⋅hr -1, p = 0.468) nor mean food consumption (slope: –0.27 ± 0.25 days⋅kJ–1, p = 0.343) was related to the length of the fattening period (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mean torpor duration was not related to the length of the fattening period.
source: Contrary to our predictions, food consumption did not significantly affect the amount of fattening (slope: 0.00 ± 0.00 g⋅kJ–1, p = 0.996), and neither mean torpor duration (slope: –0.60 ± 0.75 days⋅hr -1, p = 0.468) nor mean food consumption (slope: –0.27 ± 0.25 days⋅kJ–1, p = 0.343) was related to the length of the fattening period (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mean food consumption was not related to the length of the fattening period.
source: Contrary to our predictions, food consumption did not significantly affect the amount of fattening (slope: 0.00 ± 0.00 g⋅kJ–1, p = 0.996), and neither mean torpor duration (slope: –0.60 ± 0.75 days⋅hr -1, p = 0.468) nor mean food consumption (slope: –0.27 ± 0.25 days⋅kJ–1, p = 0.343) was related to the length of the fattening period (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the migration period, birds maintained greater morning body masses compared to the summer (3.73 ± 0.05 g).
source: In the migration period, birds maintained greater morning body masses compared to the summer (3.73 ± 0.05 g, p < 0.001), and the migration period body masses remained stable (slope: 0.00 ± 0.00 g⋅day–1, p = 0.079; Figure 1; Table 1; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on body mass measurements shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: Migration period body masses remained stable.
source: In the migration period, birds maintained greater morning body masses compared to the summer (3.73 ± 0.05 g, p < 0.001), and the migration period body masses remained stable (slope: 0.00 ± 0.00 g⋅day–1, p = 0.079; Figure 1; Table 1; Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of body mass data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: During the migration period, birds began nights with three to five times more fat than they would need to remain normothermic for the entire night at 20°C.
source: Despite beginning nights with three to five times more fat than they would need to remain normothermic for the entire night at 20°C (mean overnight fat loss on normothermic nights was 194.18 ± 4.32 mgfat in the breeding period; 196.02 ± 4.23 mgfat during fattening; and 199.22 ± 4.66 mgfat during the migration period [pairwise comparisons: p > 0.745], when accounting for the effect of night length [p < 0.001]) and not approaching the critical threshold apparent in the breeding period, birds used torpor in the migration period at similar frequencies to those of the breeding period (breeding: 61.6% ± 11.1%; migration: 65.1% ± 11.1%, p = 0.946; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is calculated from overnight fat loss measurements.

claim: Mean overnight fat loss on normothermic nights was 194.18 ± 4.32 mgfat in the breeding period, 196.02 ± 4.23 mgfat during fattening, and 199.22 ± 4.66 mgfat during the migration period.
source: Despite beginning nights with three to five times more fat than they would need to remain normothermic for the entire night at 20°C (mean overnight fat loss on normothermic nights was 194.18 ± 4.32 mgfat in the breeding period; 196.02 ± 4.23 mgfat during fattening; and 199.22 ± 4.66 mgfat during the migration period [pairwise comparisons: p > 0.745], when accounting for the effect of night length [p < 0.001]) and not approaching the critical threshold apparent in the breeding period, birds used torpor in the migration period at similar frequencies to those of the breeding period (breeding: 61.6% ± 11.1%; migration: 65.1% ± 11.1%, p = 0.946; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on body composition measurements across periods.

claim: Birds used torpor in the migration period at similar frequencies to those of the breeding period (breeding: 61.6% ± 11.1%; migration: 65.1% ± 11.1%).
source: Despite beginning nights with three to five times more fat than they would need to remain normothermic for the entire night at 20°C (mean overnight fat loss on normothermic nights was 194.18 ± 4.32 mgfat in the breeding period; 196.02 ± 4.23 mgfat during fattening; and 199.22 ± 4.66 mgfat during the migration period [pairwise comparisons: p > 0.745], when accounting for the effect of night length [p < 0.001]) and not approaching the critical threshold apparent in the breeding period, birds used torpor in the migration period at similar frequencies to those of the breeding period (breeding: 61.6% ± 11.1%; migration: 65.1% ± 11.1%, p = 0.946; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on torpor frequency measurements across periods.

claim: In the migration period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on nights when they started with greater fat stores.
source: However, in stark contrast to the breeding period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on nights when they started with greater fat stores (slope: 0.26 ± 0.11; p = 0.017) and on longer nights (slope: 2.06 ± 0.94, p = 0.028; Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of torpor propensity during the migration period.

claim: In the migration period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on longer nights.
source: However, in stark contrast to the breeding period, birds were more likely to enter torpor on nights when they started with greater fat stores (slope: 0.26 ± 0.11; p = 0.017) and on longer nights (slope: 2.06 ± 0.94, p = 0.028; Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of torpor propensity during the migration period.

claim: In the migration period, the time of torpor entry was not significantly related to evening fat content.
source: Additionally, the time of torpor entry (slope: –0.08 ± 0.07 hentry⋅%fat–1; p = 0.230), energy expenditure before torpor entry (slope: –0.06 ± 0.05 kJ⋅%fat–1; p = 0.204; Figure 3A), and overnight fat mass loss (slope: –1.54 ± 1.24 mgfat⋅%fat–1; p = 0.148; Figure 2B) were not significantly related to evening fat content.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of migration period data.

claim: In the migration period, energy expenditure before torpor entry was not significantly related to evening fat content.
source: Additionally, the time of torpor entry (slope: –0.08 ± 0.07 hentry⋅%fat–1; p = 0.230), energy expenditure before torpor entry (slope: –0.06 ± 0.05 kJ⋅%fat–1; p = 0.204; Figure 3A), and overnight fat mass loss (slope: –1.54 ± 1.24 mgfat⋅%fat–1; p = 0.148; Figure 2B) were not significantly related to evening fat content.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the migration period, overnight fat mass loss was not significantly related to evening fat content.
source: Additionally, the time of torpor entry (slope: –0.08 ± 0.07 hentry⋅%fat–1; p = 0.230), energy expenditure before torpor entry (slope: –0.06 ± 0.05 kJ⋅%fat–1; p = 0.204; Figure 3A), and overnight fat mass loss (slope: –1.54 ± 1.24 mgfat⋅%fat–1; p = 0.148; Figure 2B) were not significantly related to evening fat content.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the migration period, time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night was not significantly related to night length.
source: Time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night (slope: –0.51 ± 0.56 hentry⋅hnight–1, p = 0.333), energy expenditure before torpor entry (slope: –0.41 ± 0.41 kJ⋅hnight–1, p = 0.276), and overnight fat mass loss (slope: –0.26 ± 10.83 mgfat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.979) were consistent across the migration period and not significantly related to night length (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of migration period data.

claim: In the migration period, energy expenditure before torpor entry was not significantly related to night length.
source: Time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night (slope: –0.51 ± 0.56 hentry⋅hnight–1, p = 0.333), energy expenditure before torpor entry (slope: –0.41 ± 0.41 kJ⋅hnight–1, p = 0.276), and overnight fat mass loss (slope: –0.26 ± 10.83 mgfat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.979) were consistent across the migration period and not significantly related to night length (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of migration period data.

claim: In the migration period, overnight fat mass loss was not significantly related to night length.
source: Time of torpor entry relative to the start of the night (slope: –0.51 ± 0.56 hentry⋅hnight–1, p = 0.333), energy expenditure before torpor entry (slope: –0.41 ± 0.41 kJ⋅hnight–1, p = 0.276), and overnight fat mass loss (slope: –0.26 ± 10.83 mgfat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.979) were consistent across the migration period and not significantly related to night length (Supplementary file 1D).

source: Conversely, torpor duration was not significantly related to evening fat stores (slope: 0.10 ± 0.07 hr⋅%fat–1; p = 0.124; Figure 2A) but was positively correlated with night length (slope 1.18 ± 0.58 htorpor⋅hnight–1, p = 0.031).

claim: In the migration period, torpor duration was positively correlated with night length.
source: Conversely, torpor duration was not significantly related to evening fat stores (slope: 0.10 ± 0.07 hr⋅%fat–1; p = 0.124; Figure 2A) but was positively correlated with night length (slope 1.18 ± 0.58 htorpor⋅hnight–1, p = 0.031).

claim: Average fat content at the time of torpor entry was substantially greater in the migration period (32.94% ± 0.77%; 1249.08 ± 38.34 mgfat) compared to the breeding period.
source: In contrast to the breeding period, average fat content at the time of torpor entry was substantially greater in the migration period (32.94% ± 0.77%; 1249.08 ± 38.34 mgfat; p < 0.001; Figure 3B; Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is based on calculated fat content at torpor entry shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the migration period, there was a significant negative relationship between time of torpor entry and the fat content at that time.
source: Additionally, while there was a significant negative relationship between time of torpor entry and the fat content at that time (slope: –1.20 ± 0.35 % fat⋅hentry–1, p < 0.001; Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1D), fat content at torpor entry did not vary with night length (slope: 0.99 ± 1.41%fat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.450).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the migration period, fat content at torpor entry did not vary with night length.
source: Additionally, while there was a significant negative relationship between time of torpor entry and the fat content at that time (slope: –1.20 ± 0.35 % fat⋅hentry–1, p < 0.001; Figure 3A; Supplementary file 1D), fat content at torpor entry did not vary with night length (slope: 0.99 ± 1.41%fat⋅hnight–1, p = 0.450).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of migration period data.

claim: Ruby-throated hummingbirds exhibit substantial shifts in body composition and use of torpor between the summer breeding period and the migration period as a means to achieve premigratory fat gains.
source: Ruby-throated hummingbirds exhibit substantial shifts in body composition and use of torpor between the summer breeding period and the migration period as a means to achieve premigratory fat gains (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental findings shown in Table 1.

claim: In the summer, torpor is sensitive to critically low endogenous energy reserves.
source: In the summer, torpor is sensitive to critically low endogenous energy reserves; however, when the birds fatten for migration, this rule is abandoned, and the birds enter torpor with high levels of fat.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings comparing breeding and migration periods.

claim: When the birds fatten for migration, the low energy threshold rule is abandoned, and the birds enter torpor with high levels of fat.
source: In the summer, torpor is sensitive to critically low endogenous energy reserves; however, when the birds fatten for migration, this rule is abandoned, and the birds enter torpor with high levels of fat.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings during the migration period.

claim: The rules governing torpor use are dependent on life history stage.
source: While it does not appear that torpor initiation in the migration period is simply sensitive to a high energy threshold, the abandonment of the emergency threshold indicates that the rules governing torpor use are dependent on life history stage, and that hummingbirds may employ torpor as part of various energy management strategies throughout the annual cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed differences in torpor use between breeding and migration periods.

claim: Hummingbirds may employ torpor as part of various energy management strategies throughout the annual cycle.
source: While it does not appear that torpor initiation in the migration period is simply sensitive to a high energy threshold, the abandonment of the emergency threshold indicates that the rules governing torpor use are dependent on life history stage, and that hummingbirds may employ torpor as part of various energy management strategies throughout the annual cycle.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed flexibility in torpor use across life history stages.

claim: At air temperatures of 20°C, torpor initiation is primarily driven by instantaneous fat stores during the breeding period.
source: At air temperatures of 20°C, which free-living birds commonly experience, torpor initiation is primarily driven by instantaneous fat stores.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings during the breeding period at controlled temperature.

claim: On nights when they started with lower evening fat stores, birds depleted energy stores to critically low levels earlier in the night during the breeding period.
source: On nights when they started with lower evening fat stores birds depleted energy stores to critically low levels earlier in the night, and thus remained torpid longer, irrespective of night length.
evidence: This is based on the experimental findings during the breeding period.

claim: Torpor is an energy emergency survival strategy mechanism that protects hummingbirds from depleting energy stores during the night or before they can reach their first meal in the morning.
source: These results support the hypotheses that torpor use is sensitive to a low, consistent threshold of fat during the breeding period, and that torpor is an energy emergency survival strategy mechanism that protects hummingbirds from depleting energy stores during the night or before they can reach their first meal in the morning (Hainsworth et al., 1977; Hiebert, 1992; Powers et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental findings and citations to previous research.

claim: The threshold could occasionally be overridden to remain normothermic despite reaching critical energy levels if extended bouts of torpor on subsequent nights impede regenerative processes associated with normothermy and sleep, or increase risk of predation.
source: The threshold could occasionally be overridden to remain normothermic despite reaching critical energy levels if extended bouts of torpor on subsequent nights impede regenerative processes associated with normothermy and sleep, or increase risk of predation (Bouma et al., 2010; Carr and Lima, 2013; Hiebert, 1990).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citations to explain exceptions to the threshold rule.

claim: Hummingbirds can prematurely rewarm after inadvertent light or noise disturbances.
source: Similarly, we and other researchers have observed hummingbirds prematurely rewarming after inadvertent light or noise disturbances, which suggests that the threshold override and emergency arousal mechanisms could be related (A. Shankar, E. Eberts, personal observations).
evidence: This is based on personal observations by the authors and others.

claim: Temperature, precipitation, and food availability would likely affect free-living hummingbirds' torpor use decisions by affecting the amount of fat the birds start each night with and the rate that they expend that fat.
source: Furthermore, although temperature, precipitation, and food availability were controlled in this study, these factors would likely affect free-living hummingbirds' torpor use decisions by effecting the amount of fat the birds start each night with and the rate that they expend that fat (Hainsworth et al., 1977; McGuire et al., 2021).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about free-living birds supported by citations.

claim: If the birds were allowed to eat during the last 2 hr of the day, it is likely that they would have amassed larger evening fat stores and therefore would have entered torpor later in the night or not at all.
source: For example, the birds were fasted to ensure accurate body composition measurements, but if the birds were allowed to eat during the last 2 hr of the day, it is likely that they would have amassed larger evening fat stores and therefore would have entered torpor later in the night or not at all (Eberts et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the effect of fasting supported by a citation.

claim: At colder temperatures, normothermic hummingbirds would need to sustain a higher resting metabolic rate and may therefore anticipate an energy emergency earlier in the night.
source: For instance, free-living birds at our study site during the breeding period experienced minimum nighttime air temperatures between 10°C and 25°C (London International Airport, Ontario, Canada). At colder temperatures, normothermic hummingbirds would need to sustain a higher resting metabolic rate and may therefore anticipate an energy emergency earlier in the night (Hiebert, 1990).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the effect of temperature supported by a citation.

claim: The evidence strongly supports the existence of an 'adipostat' mechanism that initiates compensatory physiological changes depending on the instantaneous level of endogenous energy stores.
source: While these factors likely play a role in the complex decision-making that governs free-living hummingbird torpor use during the breeding season, our evidence strongly supports the existence of an 'adipostat' mechanism that initiates compensatory physiological changes depending on the instantaneous level of endogenous energy stores (Boyer and Barnes, 1999; Powers et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and supported by citations.

claim: During the migration period, hummingbirds appear to enter torpor after a consistent amount of time, so that they expend a predictable amount of energy and achieve greater energy savings as they experience progressively longer nights in the late summer.
source: Instead of initiating torpor to survive the night whenever they reach a critically low threshold, hummingbirds appear to enter torpor after a consistent amount of time, so that they expend a predictable amount of energy and achieve greater energy savings as they experience progressively longer nights in the late summer.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings during the migration period.

claim: During the migration period, birds must remain normothermic for a consistent period of time, perhaps accounting for the time it takes to process their final evening meal and their blood sugar declines to a level allowing for torpor initiation.
source: This suggests that during the migration period, birds maximize their time in torpor, but must remain normothermic for a consistent period of time, perhaps accounting for the time it takes to process their final evening meal and their blood sugar declines to a level allowing for torpor initiation (Eberts et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: The normothermic period before torpor could allow the birds to achieve sufficient sleep before entering torpor when the regenerative and immunological benefits of sleep are unlikely to occur.
source: This normothermic period could also allow the birds to achieve sufficient sleep before entering torpor when the regenerative and immunological benefits of sleep are unlikely to occur (Bouma et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by a citation.

claim: The seasonal change in torpor use shows that torpor is a critical energy management strategy that allows migratory hummingbirds to balance fuel supply and demand during a particular season.
source: Overall, the seasonal change in torpor use, from a survival strategy initiated by an 'adipostat' mechanism to a more routine use of torpor to maximize energy savings and build fat stores prior to migration, shows that torpor is a critical energy management strategy that allows migratory hummingbirds to balance fuel supply and demand during a particular season.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Similar torpor use patterns have been well studied in mammals.
source: Similar torpor use patterns have been well studied in mammals, though studies investigating avian endocrine mechanisms are needed to elucidate the proximate factors of torpor initiation across taxa.
evidence: This is a general statement about the literature on mammalian torpor.

claim: Studies investigating avian endocrine mechanisms are needed to elucidate the proximate factors of torpor initiation across taxa.
source: Similar torpor use patterns have been well studied in mammals, though studies investigating avian endocrine mechanisms are needed to elucidate the proximate factors of torpor initiation across taxa.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the current findings.

claim: The similarities between the life histories of North American hummingbirds and bats provide an important lens through which to interrogate the ultimate drivers of torpor use throughout the annual cycle.
source: The similarities between the life histories of North American hummingbirds and bats provide an important lens through which to interrogate the ultimate drivers of torpor use throughout the annual cycle (McGuire et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Using torpor while roosting could allow both hummingbirds and bats to maintain high fuel stores when feeding opportunities are constrained by migratory priorities.
source: Using torpor while roosting could allow both hummingbirds and bats animals to maintain high fuel stores when feeding opportunities are constrained by migratory priorities.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the function of torpor in migrants.

claim: Ruby-throated hummingbirds are diurnal migrants that do not forage at night.
source: Unlike most nocturnal migrant birds that can replenish fuel stores during the day, ruby-throated hummingbirds are diurnal migrants that do not forage at night.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the species' behavior.

claim: North American bats migrate at night when they would otherwise forage and do not forage during the day.
source: In an opposite but parallel manner, North American bats migrate at night when they would otherwise forage and do not forage during the day.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bat behavior.

claim: In both hummingbirds and bats, foraging, migrating, and sleeping can be mutually exclusive endeavors, but torpor can allow them to conserve energy and avoid making extended refueling stopovers.
source: In both of these types of animals, foraging, migrating, and sleeping can be mutually exclusive endeavors, but torpor can allow them to conserve energy and avoid making extended refueling stopovers (McGuire et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The drastic shift in the relationship between hummingbird body composition and torpor use, and of the link between torpor duration and mass gains in the late summer compellingly support the 'torpor-assisted migration' hypothesis.
source: While we did not study free-living birds while they migrated, the drastic shift in the relationship between hummingbird body composition and torpor use, and of the link between torpor duration and mass gains in the late summer compellingly support the 'torpor-assisted migration' hypothesis (Carpenter and Hixon, 1988; Hiebert, 1993; Hou and Welch, 2016; McGuire et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and supported by citations.

source: The magnitude and timing of fattening in our captive birds resembled those documented in some free-living ruby-throated hummingbirds (present study: 0.58 ± 0.05 g, 19.6% ± 1.6% over 10 ± 1 days; Hou and Welch, 2016: ~ 0.65 g, or 17% over 4 days).

source: The ranges in magnitude and timing of fattening are not surprising because hummingbirds are asocial birds that do not migrate in flocks, and we would not expect them to have finely synchronized timing of migratory preparation, especially in the absence of natural ecological cues.

claim: Birds will enter torpor when their fat stores reach a consistently low fat threshold (5%), during life history stages where a relatively lean body composition is advantageous.
